name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPA-16P 'Piston Sixteen'
description:
The KPA-16P is mechanically identical to the KPA-16 from the handguard forward, but the gas system has been redesigned around a short-stroke piston and op-rod arrangement that keeps propellant gases out of the receiver entirely. The bolt carrier group runs cooler, cleaner, and with a notably different cycling impulse — slightly heavier and more deliberate, which some operators describe as 'slower but honest.' The gas block is a fixed low-profile unit that doesn't adjust, which Kang-Petrov's engineers argue is a reliability feature since adjustable gas blocks require maintenance most Tier 1–2 buyers don't perform. The barrel is 16.5 inches, hammer-forged, and rated for sustained fire that would cook a standard DI barrel's chrome lining in a comparable time frame.

The piston variant was developed specifically for GLMZ's lakefront and waterway zones where humidity, rain, and the occasional submersion event make direct impingement reliability less theoretical and more immediately career-ending. Slagworks markets it with a small premium over the base KPA-16 — maybe 15% more Quanta — which puts it right at the upper edge of comfortable Tier 1 spending. Buyers tend to be waterway workers, dock security, and people operating in the GLMZ's extensive underground drainage infrastructure who need a rifle that doesn't care if it's been sitting in condensation for six hours.

The KPA-16P's piston assembly makes a distinctive metallic clunk during cycling that experienced ears can distinguish from the softer reciprocating sound of a DI gun. In the quiet of a drainage tunnel or an abandoned lakefront processing facility, that sound carries. Street operators who work those environments have started calling it the 'wet sixteen' not because of the environment it's designed for, but because the cycling sound reminds them of something mechanical moving through water. It's an unfair name for a reliable tool, but names stick regardless of fairness.
specifications:
caliber: 5.56mm Combat Standard
effective_range: 400m
rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic
magazine_capacity: 30 rounds
weight: 3.4 kg
tactical_use: The KPA-16P fills the same general-purpose carbine role as the base KPA-16 but is specifically optimized for wet, dirty, or suppressed-fire applications. The piston system significantly reduces carbon buildup in the receiver, which matters when operators are running suppressors in close environments — DI guns running suppressed in enclosed spaces can become unreliable within a single magazine; the P-model runs significantly longer before requiring attention. Operators in drainage corridors and lakefront zones favor it for sustained defensive use where cleaning between engagements isn't possible.
cultural_context: Among GLMZ's waterway and drainage infrastructure workers — a class of laborers who exist in the literal underbelly of the megacity — the KPA-16P has developed a specific reputation as a tool that works where other tools don't. The premium over the base model is real but not prohibitive, and in communities where your operating environment is inherently hostile to most firearms, that premium buys something tangible. Mids who buy the P-model for dry-environment use are sometimes gently mocked by the working waterway crowd for spending the extra Quanta without needing it.
story_hooks: A KPA-16P is recovered from a sealed drainage maintenance access point beneath a Zheng-dao Bioelectric facility — the weapon was wrapped in oil cloth, loaded, and hidden there recently enough that the rounds show no corrosion, suggesting someone stashed it in anticipation of a specific event that hasn't happened yet.

A waterway worker's cooperative is offering double the market rate for KPA-16P piston assemblies only, no questions asked — someone in that cooperative is converting a large number of base KPA-16 rifles to piston operation, which implies either a very well-funded preparation project or a supply of stripped lowers that shouldn't exist.
